trial.title: Acupuncture Versus Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation on Pain Post Upper Abdominal Surgeries

endpoints.measure: assessment of change of postoperative quality of recovery
endpoints.description: The Postoperative Quality of Recovery Scale is a verbal scale designed to assess the quality of recovery in six domains: physiology, nociceptive, emotional, activities of daily living, cognitive, and overall patient perspective. It measures systolic blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and airway control, aiming to assess physiologic safety and home readiness for day care surgery. It also assesses pain and nausea using a 1-5% Likert rating scale. Emotional domain measures feelings of anxiety and depression. Activities of daily living assess physical return to normality through daily activities, with scores ranging from 3 to 1. Cognitive domain measures orientation, verbal memory, executive functioning, attention, and concentration. Performance variability tolerance factors are applied to ensure participants are not included in subsequent analysis if baseline scores are equal to or less than the tolerance factor.

endpoints.measure: assessment of change of pressure pain threshold
endpoints.description: An algometer is a handheld device used for pressure tolerance testing, typically with a 1-cm2 pressure application surface and force readings in newtons or kilograms. It has a resolution of 0.2 newton, 250-newton capacity, and a 1000-Hz sampling rate. The device is designed to measure pains and track recovery/healing, and is tested for high reliability and validity compared to force plate readings.

Small sample size (n=40) limits power to detect between-group differences. Primary endpoint likely to show improvement in both groups; statistical superiority of one intervention over the other is uncertain.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT07036393 is a single-blind randomized controlled trial comparing acupuncture versus transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for postoperative pain management after upper abdominal surgeries (laparoscopic cholecystectomy, gastrectomy).

Primary endpoint: Postoperative Quality of Recovery Scale (PQRS) assessing change from baseline to 4 weeks across six domains (physiology, nociceptive, emotional, activities of daily living, cognitive, overall patient perspective).
Secondary endpoint: Pressure pain threshold measured by algometer at baseline and 4 weeks.

Evidence retrieved: (1) Meta-analysis of 76 RCTs (n=9,665) on TEAS for postoperative pain showing WMD -14.60 mg morphine equivalent reduction and improved recovery outcomes (PMC11092893); (2) Meta-analysis of 28 RCTs on TEAS for laparoscopy postoperative pain showing effective pain relief and reduced hospitalization (PMC8783713); (3) Pilot study on personalized checkpoint acupuncture showing 86% VAS reduction and 64% pain threshold increase after abdominal surgery (PMC10562323); (4) Protocol on TEAS combined with electroacupuncture for abdominal surgery recovery (PMC9703060).

Evidence-role assessment: PMC11092893 - indirect_direction (TEAS efficacy for postoperative pain, different endpoint measures); PMC8783713 - indirect_direction (TEAS for laparoscopy pain, similar population); PMC10562323 - indirect_direction (acupuncture for abdominal surgery pain, pressure algometry outcome matches secondary endpoint); PMC9703060 - mechanism_background (combined TEAS+EA protocol).
Population match: Adults 20-45 years undergoing upper abdominal surgery. Evidence from general abdominal surgery and laparoscopy populations applicable with moderate confidence.
Endpoint match: PQRS is validated for postoperative recovery assessment. Pressure pain threshold is objective measure used in acupuncture/TENS studies.

Treatment comparison: Both acupuncture and TENS have demonstrated efficacy for postoperative pain in meta-analyses. Head-to-head comparison evidence is limited; most studies compare each to sham or usual care.

Prediction rationale: Both interventions are expected to show improvement from baseline in PQRS scores and pressure pain threshold based on established efficacy in similar populations. Between-group differences are uncertain due to lack of direct comparative trials.
Primary uncertainty: No direct head-to-head RCTs comparing acupuncture versus TENS for upper abdominal surgery with PQRS endpoint. Sample size (n=40) is small for detecting between-group differences.
Secondary uncertainty: Optimal measurement protocol for pressure pain threshold postoperatively not standardized; timing and anatomical location may affect results.
